name: Times club monthly special crossword No 20,270

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Literally the last couple, retired, each awfully shy, visiting privates’ joint

indicators.note: to retire is to draw back, so the pair of letters is taken in the backwards order
done awfully means done badly, so the word that follows is jumbled
a visitor goes inside someone's place, so these pieces sit within the soldiers

blocks.note: literally, the last two letters of the alphabet
GIs are American private soldiers; split around the inserted letters
'a pop' means each, as in five pounds a pop
taken as written, then jumbled

explanation.surface: A coy pair at the back of the queue awkwardly sharing a joint with some soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Literally' means the letters themselves: the alphabet's final pair. 'A pop' is the colloquial each, as in a pound a pop, and 'privates' are American soldiers, not body parts.
explanation.definitionFit: A zygapophysis is an articular process of a vertebra, one of the bony projections forming the small joints of the spine.

clue.text: What’s not unique in puzzles these days? Like fresh compiler for star publication

indicators.note: something made fresh is made anew, so the word before it is reworked

blocks.note: the only letter that appears twice in the word puzzles
AD, anno Domini, marks the present era
taken as written, then jumbled

explanation.surface: A setter wonders what is common in modern crosswords and suggests a fresh astrologer.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening question reads as a remark about crosswords, but it points to the doubled letter in the word puzzles.
explanation.definitionFit: Zadkiel was the pen name of Richard Morrison, who compiled a famous Victorian astrological almanac predicting events from the stars.

clue.text: State to jail revolutionary and an informant

indicators.note: a revolution turns things round, so the word for prison is read backwards

blocks.note: jug is slang for prison
the indefinite article
a rat is someone who informs on others

explanation.surface: A government locks up a rebel and a police informer.
explanation.definitionFit: Gujarat is a state on the west coast of India.

clue.text: Ten large square sandwiches, ace kept until last with a rich tomato sauce!

indicators.note: keeping something until last takes it out of its place and holds it back for the end
a sandwich has filling between its slices, so the first pieces go inside the square

blocks.note: a piazza is an Italian town square; its first A is moved, as 'ace kept until last' says
ten written as the digits 1 and 0, read as letters
L is the abbreviation for large
A is the abbreviation for ace, kept until the end

explanation.surface: Ten big pizzas sandwiching ace toppings, saved till last, in plenty of tomato sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: PIAZZA moves its first A to the end, and the gap before that A takes IO and L. The pizza in the square is a nice coincidence.
explanation.definitionFit: Alla pizzaiola means cooked pizza-maker's style, in a rich sauce of tomatoes, garlic and oregano.

clue.text: Aberdonian dodges pledges with alternative tip from notebook

indicators.note: an alternative is swapped in, so one letter of the word is replaced by another

blocks.note: pawns are items left as pledges for a loan
the other tip of the word, its last letter, replaces the first-letter tip

explanation.surface: A Scot avoids promises by jotting down a different tip in a notebook.
explanation.walkthrough: Notebook has two tips: its first letter N in PAWNS is replaced by its other tip, K.
explanation.definitionFit: Pawk is a Scots word for a trick or wile, so pawks are crafty dodges in a Scottish speaker's mouth.

clue.text: Aggressive behaviour of brother rising to grab pupil once again!

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means reading upwards, so the exclamation is turned backwards
grabbing something holds it, so the other pieces go inside

blocks.note: 'Brother!' and 'My!' are both exclamations of surprise
an OB, old boy, is a former pupil of a school
bis is the musical direction to repeat

explanation.surface: A sibling bursts up to grab a former schoolmate, misbehaving all over again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brother' looks like a sibling, but it is the exclamation, swapped for its equal, MY.
explanation.definitionFit: Yobbism is loutish, rowdy conduct of the kind associated with yobs, British slang for hooligans.

clue.text: A number of physics standards people present favourably

blocks.note: the International Organization for Standardization
to spin a story is to present it in a favourable light

explanation.surface: Several people who set physics standards make it sound good.
explanation.definitionFit: Isospin is a quantum number in particle physics, used to group protons and neutrons as states of one particle.

clue.text: Artefact of value to Victor, but jeered outrageously

indicators.note: acting outrageously means behaving wildly, so the letters before it run riot

blocks.note: taken as written
V is Victor in the radio alphabet
taken as written, part of the jumbled letters

explanation.surface: A prized ornament goes to Victor, though he was booed for it.
explanation.definitionFit: An objet de vertu is a small, finely made curio prized for its craftsmanship, such as a snuffbox.

clue.text: City where Miss Clare and Jarndyce originally come together in Dickens

indicators.note: originally points to the start of the name, so only its opening letter is kept
the two pieces gather inside the novelist's pen name, enclosed by it

blocks.note: Boz was the pen name Dickens used for his early sketches
Ada Clare is a ward in Chancery in Bleak House
the opening letter of John Jarndyce, her guardian in the same novel

explanation.surface: A reading of Bleak House, where two of its characters finally meet in a city.
explanation.walkthrough: Ada Clare and John Jarndyce are both from Bleak House, and Boz was the young Dickens's pen name, so every name in the surface belongs to one author.
explanation.definitionFit: Badajoz is a Spanish city near the Portuguese border, famous for its siege during the Peninsular War.

clue.text: First person with book to pay for one of eg Donald’s plates?

blocks.note: the first person plural pronoun
B is the abbreviation for book
to foot the bill is to pay for it

explanation.surface: Some of us, with a book, must pay for the dishes Donald eats from.
explanation.walkthrough: Plates are feet in rhyming slang (plates of meat), and Donald is Donald Duck, whose feet are webbed.
explanation.definitionFit: A duck's foot has skin stretched between its toes, so Donald Duck's plates, in the slang sense, are webbed ones.

clue.text: Touches on-screen key, weirdly unsettling confused Glaswegian

blocks.note: to tap is to touch lightly
Alt is a computer keyboard key
eerie means strange and unnerving

explanation.surface: Someone tapping keys on a screen finds it strangely disturbing and gets muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confused' looks like an anagram signal but is part of the definition, a Scottish word for topsy-turvy.
explanation.definitionFit: Tapsalteerie is Scots for upside down or in disorder, so it is how a Glaswegian might say muddled.

clue.text: State there’s some merit rearming

indicators.note: some means only a portion, so the answer is a run of letters inside the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words, dropping the first and last two

explanation.surface: A country argues it is partly justified in rebuilding its army.
explanation.definitionFit: Eritrea is a sovereign country in the Horn of Africa, on the Red Sea coast.

clue.text: Small family with dad shooting up

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
kin are relatives
an informal word for father

explanation.surface: A little household with a father whose children are growing fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shooting up' suggests growing children, but here it is drug slang for injection.
explanation.definitionFit: Skin-popping is slang for injecting a drug under the skin rather than into a vein, a form of drug use.

clue.text: Class member read from the right commercial reading material

indicators.note: reading from right to left turns the word that follows backwards

blocks.note: a commercial is an advertisement
lit is short for literature

explanation.surface: Someone in a class reads an advert backwards along with their set texts.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dalit is a member of the lowest group in India's caste system, formerly called untouchables, so a member of a social class.

clue.text: Answer shortly coming back on pensioners wanting a thing for a dish

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the pensioners go without the next letter
coming back means returning, so the two pieces before it are read in the opposite direction
in an across clue, X on Y puts X after Y, so the reversed piece is sent second, behind the pensioners

blocks.note: OAPs are old age pensioners
the letter that the pensioners lose
A is the abbreviation for answer
in a mo, short for in a moment, means shortly

explanation.surface: A reply about pensioners who fancy one particular dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' in an across clue places the reversed piece after the pensioners. A 'thing' is an obsession, as in having a thing for chocolate.
explanation.definitionFit: Opsomania is an abnormal craving for one particular food, an obsessive passion for a single kind of meal.

clue.text: Segment of bone from back: in time, black

indicators.note: in places the colour inside the period of time

blocks.note: the stern is the back of a ship
an era is a period of time; it is split around the inserted letter
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A doctor describes a piece of bone from someone's back that turned black over time.
explanation.definitionFit: A sternebra is one of the segments that fuse to form the breastbone, a section of skeleton.

clue.text: Minister’s office requiring alternative to wits and class

blocks.note: viz and ie are both written in place of 'to wit', meaning namely
a rate is a class or grade, as in first-rate

explanation.surface: A government post that needs a different kind of intelligence, plus some style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wits' looks like cleverness, but it is the plural of 'to wit', and its two stand-ins are VIZ and IE.
explanation.definitionFit: A vizier was a high minister in Muslim states such as the Ottoman Empire; the vizierate is that post or term of office.

clue.text: Compound of nitrogen that’s apparently turned yellow above cottage

blocks.note: N is the symbol for nitrogen; turned on its side, the letter looks like a Z
or is gold or yellow in heraldry
a gîte is a French holiday cottage

explanation.surface: A chemist notes a nitrogen compound that seems to have turned yellow, on display above a cottage.
explanation.walkthrough: Rotating the printed N by a quarter turn gives the shape of Z; 'apparently' admits this is visual, not chemical.
explanation.definitionFit: Zorgite is a mineral, a selenide of lead and copper, so a naturally occurring chemical compound.

clue.text: Goes down to clean up unemployment money: euro, initially, then two shillings

indicators.note: initially points to the beginnings, so each word gives only its opening letter
in a down clue up means read from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the first letter of each of the three words
a bob was an old British shilling, so two of them are bobs

explanation.surface: Someone stoops to tidy up their dole money: some euros and a couple of shillings.
explanation.definitionFit: Emu-bob is Australian slang for walking bent over to pick up litter, like an emu pecking, so bending to tidy.

clue.text: Quote you might pick up is great deal

indicators.note: picking something up by ear means hearing it, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: to quote a source is to cite it

explanation.surface: A quotation overheard turns out to be a bargain.
explanation.definitionFit: Used adverbially, 'a sight' means a lot, as in 'a sight better', matching a great deal.

clue.text: Celebrated driving supporter in need of lift for pre-match do

indicators.note: in a down clue lifting something raises it, so the word is read from the bottom up

blocks.note: to sing someone's praises is to celebrate them
a golf tee supports the ball for a drive

explanation.surface: A famous golfer's caddie needs a lift before the match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pre-match' suggests sport, but the match is a marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A sangeet is a musical party held before a South Asian wedding, a celebration ahead of the marriage.

clue.text: Way of spelling sound defeat: one’s packed golf clubs!

indicators.note: packed into means placed inside, so the two pieces go between the golf letters

blocks.note: G is Golf in the radio alphabet
a loss is a defeat
I is the Roman numeral one
C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games

explanation.surface: A golfer in defeat packs away the clubs.
explanation.definitionFit: Glossic is a phonetic spelling system devised by Alexander Ellis, a way of writing words as they are pronounced.

clue.text: Marine mammal tailed ferry, perhaps, by virtue of being close to hull

indicators.note: to tail something is to cut off its end, so the ferry loses its final letter
the close of a word is its end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: a ro-ro is a roll-on roll-off ferry
qua is Latin for in the capacity of
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A whale follows a ferry, swimming close to its hull.
explanation.definitionFit: A rorqual is any of the baleen whales with throat grooves, such as the blue whale, a sea mammal.

clue.text: Stop second melody being broadcast?

indicators.note: broadcast words are heard over the air, so the pieces are taken by sound

blocks.note: a lay is a song or ballad
second place is number two

explanation.surface: A radio presenter cuts off the second song mid-broadcast.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay to is a nautical phrase for bringing a ship to a halt facing the wind.

clue.text: Stratford constable’s blunder: bad omen arresting corporal?

indicators.note: bad suggests something gone wrong, so the word that follows is jumbled
arresting someone means holding them, so the soldier is held inside

blocks.note: taken as written, then jumbled
a corporal is a non-commissioned officer

explanation.surface: A police officer's mistake is a bad sign when a soldier is arrested.
explanation.walkthrough: The Stratford constable is Dogberry in Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing, famous for misusing long words.
explanation.definitionFit: Dogberry says non-come, a garbled version of the Latin non compos mentis, so the word is literally his slip of the tongue.

clue.text: Do buy in fragments for moulded component

indicators.note: broken into fragments, the words are shattered and their letters rebuilt in a new order

blocks.note: the letters of these words, plus the IN beside them, are jumbled
taken as written, part of the jumbled letters

explanation.surface: Advice to purchase a moulded part in pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A unibody is a vehicle or device shell formed as a single moulded or machined part rather than assembled from several.

clue.text: Pinkish weed — ruby if turned at intervals — in American’s jar?

indicators.note: turned round means facing the other way, so the run of letters is read backwards
taking letters at regular intervals means keeping every other one

blocks.note: every second letter of these words is kept

explanation.surface: A reddish weed, coloured ruby, if you turn it, sits in an American's jar.
explanation.walkthrough: A jar is British slang for a glass of beer, which the American slang word also means.
explanation.definitionFit: Brewski is American slang for a beer, which a British drinker would call a jar.

clue.text: Shocked into moving from Home Counties, leads a cloistered life?

blocks.note: the Home Counties surround London in the South East of England
someone who leads a cloistered life is monastic

explanation.surface: Someone shaken into leaving the commuter belt to become a monk.
explanation.definitionFit: Seismonastic describes a plant's movement in response to shaking or touch, as when a mimosa folds its leaves.
